analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-style public health plan automatically covering every child born after 2004 through age 23.
analysis.headline: A bill to give every child born after 2004 government health coverage from birth gathered 85 cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have automatically enrolled every child born after 2004 in a new federal health plan called MediKids, modeled on Medicare, covering doctor visits, screenings, hospital care, and prescriptions until age 23. Families would pay a monthly premium through their tax return, with full exemptions and reductions for low-income families and no cost-sharing for the poorest children. Families with other coverage could opt out, and the public plan would remain as a safety net whenever that coverage lapsed.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children — especially the more than 9 million uninsured children cited in the bill's findings — gain guaranteed coverage that follows them across state lines and survives job changes, income swings, and losses of private insurance. Pediatricians, hospitals, and community health providers would see fewer unpaid visits and fewer children arriving sick at emergency rooms.

how_it_helps.text: Children born after December 31, 2004 would be deemed enrolled at birth, with coverage continuing until age 23, so no child could fall through gaps in private insurance [S3].
The benefit package must include Medicare's core benefits, all mandatory Medicaid benefits including early and periodic screening and diagnostic services, and prescription drugs [S2] [S3].

Families below 150% of the poverty line would pay no premiums or cost-sharing, and the premium is capped at 5% of adjusted gross income for everyone else, with exemptions for very low-income taxpayers [S3].
A refundable tax credit would cover 50% of out-of-pocket cost-sharing for eligible families [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Families with enrolled children would pay a monthly premium collected through the tax system, though low-income families are exempt or pay reduced amounts. Because premiums cover only about a quarter of estimated per-person costs, the bill directs the Treasury Secretary to propose a gradual schedule of progressive tax changes to cover the rest as enrollment grows — meaning higher-income taxpayers would bear an unspecified share of the long-term cost.

drawbacks.text: The financing is left open: premiums cover only 25% of estimated annual per-capita costs, and the bill merely directs Treasury to propose progressive tax changes later, so the true long-term cost to taxpayers was never specified [S3].

The new entitlement would be phased in over five years by expanding age eligibility gradually, meaning full coverage would not arrive until late in the decade and future Congresses could slow or alter the rollout [S3].

Critics of public-plan expansions argue a free or cheap default public plan draws employers and families away from private coverage, shrinking the private insurance pool — though the bill lets families with equivalent coverage opt out with a zero premium [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — universal, portable health coverage for an entire generation of children — is large and directly targets the 9 million uninsured children Congress itself cited. The main cost is real but diffuse: higher taxes whose exact shape was left for later, and a modest new premium on enrolled families, shielded for the poorest. The bill's honesty about its unfunded long-term financing was also its political weakness, giving committees a reason to shelve it without a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, was sent to the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 11, 2003 by Rep. Pete Stark and referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees [S1] [S5].
It gathered 85 cosponsors — 83 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent [S4].
On March 24-25, 2003 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 108th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were spared any new public competition for children's coverage, and taxpayers faced no new program cost — while the families of uninsured children remained uninsured.

for.name: Rep. Pete Stark
for.role: House Ways and Means Committee member; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a broad slate of cosponsors to create a Medicare-style automatic health plan for all children born after 2004.

for.name: 85 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support — 83 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chairman of the committee with first jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in the Health Subcommittee from March 2003 until the Congress ended with no action [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or scheduled any consideration during the 108th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic — 83 of 85 cosponsors — with a single Republican and a single Independent; the committees controlled by the Republican majority took no action.

industries.note: A free-default public plan competing with private coverage would draw customers away from insurers, though the bill lets families with equivalent private coverage opt out and lets plans participate under Medicare+Choice-style rules. Insurers had a direct financial interest in the bill never advancing.

industries.industry: Hospitals, pediatricians, and children's health providers
industries.note: Universal children's coverage would replace unpaid care and bad debt with Medicare-style payment, and provider participation agreements would apply. Their gain runs alongside children getting care.

The bill requires prescription drug and biological coverage for all enrollees, creating a large new pool of insured young patients, though payments would follow Medicare-style reimbursement rates that pay less than private insurance.
